proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(G_0=h_1\circ h_0^{-1}\).  The pushforward identities in ass:cic-identification give
\[
G_0\#P_{C0}=(h_1\circ h_0^{-1})\#(h_0\#\nu_C)=h_1\#\nu_C=P_{C1}.
\]
We first record why the cyclic-monotonicity premise is enough, rather than assuming optimality.  If \(\Gamma\) is a compact \(c_{\mathbb T}\)-cyclically monotone graph, fix \((x_0,z_0)\in\Gamma\) and define the usual chain potential
\[
u(x)=\inf_{m\geq 1}\ \inf_{(x_r,z_r)\in\Gamma}
 \left\{c_{\mathbb T}(x,z_m)-c_{\mathbb T}(x_m,z_m)
 +\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\bigl[c_{\mathbb T}(x_{r+1},z_r)-c_{\mathbb T}(x_r,z_r)\bigr]\right\},
\]
where \(x_{m+1}=x\).  The cyclic inequalities prevent the infimum from being \(-\infty\).  With
\(v(z)=\inf_x\{c_{\mathbb T}(x,z)-u(x)\}\), the chain construction gives
\(u(x)+v(z)\leq c_{\mathbb T}(x,z)\) everywhere and equality on \(\Gamma\).  Hence every coupling supported by \(\Gamma\) attains equality between the primal cost and the dual value \(\int u\,dP_{C0}+\int v\,dP_{C1}\), and is optimal.  Thus the coupling induced by \(G_0\) is optimal.  The uniqueness built into the definition of \(\operatorname{OT}\) therefore yields
\[
p=G_0=h_1\circ h_0^{-1}\qquad P_{C0}\text{-almost everywhere}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
q=p\#P_{T0}=(h_1\circ h_0^{-1})\#(h_0\#\nu_T)=h_1\#\nu_T.
\]
Likewise \(G_1=h_1\circ h_{1\star}^{-1}\) pushes \(P_{T1}=h_{1\star}\#\nu_T\) to \(q\); its graph is cyclically monotone, so the same argument and uniqueness give
\[
T=G_1=h_1\circ h_{1\star}^{-1}qquad P_{T1}\text{-almost everywhere}.
\]
The four displayed equalities use only ass:cic-identification, the pushforward definition, and optimal-map uniqueness.

The margin in ass:lift-regularity is strictly larger than \(\beta\).  Therefore every sufficiently small \(C^1\) perturbation of \(p\) and \(T\) remains at least \(\beta/2\) from the cost cut relation and retains the same representatives of the half-open translation cells.  The triples selected in def:translation-aware-lift are consequently locally stable.  For a treated rank \(u\), the observed post outcome is \(y=h_{1\star}(u)\), whereas its no-treatment post outcome is
\[
h_1(u)=(h_1\circ h_{1\star}^{-1})(y)=T(y).
\]
Thus the causal displacement is \(y-T(y)\).  In the selected equivariant lift this is
\(\widetilde y-\widetilde T(\widetilde y)=-a_T-\nabla\phi_T(\widetilde y)\), independently of the representative \(\widetilde y\).  Evaluation at the declared grid proves the stated equality with \(\tau(P)\), and distinguishes the causal displacement from the observed-law construction that identifies it.

Write \(a=f_{C0}\), \(b=f_{C1}\), \(r=f_{T0}\), and \(t=f_{T1}\).  We first dispose of the harmonic component without silently imposing a normalization.  The chain construction in the proof of lem:torus-cic-identification supplies a single-valued torus potential \(u_F\) satisfying dual equality on the graph of every optimal map \(F\).  On the cut-free smooth branch, differentiating that equality in its first coordinate gives
\[
\nabla u_F(x)=\partial_x c_{\mathbb T}(x,F(x))=x-\widetilde F(x),
\]
where the chosen lift difference is the unique shortest displacement.  Thus \(\widetilde F(x)-x=-\nabla u_F(x)\) is the gradient of a periodic function.  Comparing with \(\widetilde F(x)-x=a_F+\nabla\phi_F(x)\) and integrating over the torus gives \(a_F=0\).  Hence \(a_p=a_T=0\) throughout a sufficiently small regular path, so
\[
\dot a_p=\dot a_T=0,
\qquad
\mathcal H_P[\delta]=0.
\tag{1}
\]
This also proves the asserted cellwise Riesz representation: every harmonic score is the zero function and has \(L^2(P_g)\)-norm zero.

Let \(u\) and \(v\) be the mean-zero derivatives of the periodic inner and outer potentials.  Differentiating
\[
b(p(x))\det S(x)=a(x)
\]
and using \(D\det(S)[D^2u]=\operatorname{cof}(S):D^2u\), together with \(\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{cof}S)=0\), which follows by differentiating the two-by-two cofactor entries and commuting mixed derivatives, gives
\[
\delta_{C0}=det(S)\,\delta_{C1}\circ p+operatorname{div}(aS^{-1}\nabla u).
\]
Since \(A=aS^{-1}\), this is
\[
\mathcal L_Au=\det(S)\,\delta_{C1}\circ p-\delta_{C0}.
\tag{2}
\]
Set \(w=u\circ R_0\).  The divergence change-of-variables formula
\[
\det(D)\{\operatorname{div}_x Z\}\circ R_0
=\operatorname{div}_y\{\det(D)D^{-1}Z\circ R_0\}
\]
applied to (2), and \(p\circ R_0=T\), gives
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathsf C}w=e_{C1}-e_{C0},
\qquad
w=\mathcal L_{\mathsf C}^{-1}\Pi_0(e_{C1}-e_{C0}).
\tag{3}
\]
The right side has mean zero because it is the pullback of the difference of two density tangents; the displayed \(\Pi_0\) also makes the inverse well typed.

For a smooth test function \(\zeta\), differentiating the pushforward identity yields
\[
\left.\partial_\epsilon\right|_0\int\zeta\,d(p_\epsilon\#P_{T0,\epsilon})
=\int\zeta(p(x))\delta_{T0}(x)\,dx
\int\nabla\zeta(p(x))\cdot\nabla u(x)r(x)\,dx.
\]
Integration by parts, justified by periodicity, therefore gives
\[
\dot q=p\#\delta_{T0}-\operatorname{div}_z\{q(z)\nabla u(p^{-1}(z))\}.
\tag{4}
\]
Differentiating \(q(T(y))\det H(y)=t(y)\), using (4), and applying the displayed divergence change-of-variables identity once more gives
\[
\mathcal L_Bv=e_{T0}-e_{T1}
-\operatorname{div}\{BD^{-\mathsf T}\nabla w\}.
\tag{5}
\]

It remains to verify the coefficient identity, including every Jacobian.  From \(D=S(R_0)^{-1}H\), symmetry of the two Brenier Jacobians, and \(A=f_{C0}S^{-1}\),
\[
\mathsf C
=f_{C0}(R_0)\det(D)H^{-1}S(R_0)H^{-1}.
\]
Moreover, the two change-of-variables equations imply
\[
t=f_{T0}(R_0)\det(D)=\alpha f_{C0}(R_0)\det(D).
\]
Thus
\[
BD^{-\mathsf T}
=tH^{-1}S(R_0)H^{-1}=\alpha\mathsf C.
\tag{6}
\]
Substituting (3) and (6) into (5), and expanding the divergence, yields
\[
\mathcal L_Bv
=\alpha(e_{C1}-e_{C0})+e_{T0}-e_{T1}
-(\mathsf C\nabla\alpha)\cdot
 \nabla\mathcal L_{\mathsf C}^{-1}\Pi_0(e_{C1}-e_{C0}).
\tag{7}
\]
The mean-zero projection may be inserted before each inverse because gradients annihilate constants.  The derivative of the selected lifted outer map is \(\dot a_T+\nabla v=\nabla v\) by (1).  Evaluating (7) on \(\mathcal Y_J\) proves exactly the formula for \(\mathcal D_P\) and \(\mathcal H_P\) in the statement.  Subtracting (2) and (5) at two nearby density tuples, the identity \(\det(M+E)-\det M=\operatorname{cof}(M):E+\det E\) makes the residual quadratic in the density and map increments.  The normalized uniformly elliptic inverses therefore bound that residual by \(C\lVert\delta\rVert_{C^{s-2}}^2\).  This proves Frechet, rather than merely directional, differentiability.

For completeness, the second term has a bounded score.  Uniform ellipticity makes each gradient Green kernel bounded by \(C d(x,z)^{-1}\).  Its kernel is a convolution of two such kernels against the smooth factor \(\mathsf C\nabla\alpha\), and the elementary split into \(d(x,z)\leq d(x,u)/2\), \(d(z,u)\leq d(x,u)/2\), and the complement gives
\[
\left|\int_{\mathbb T^2}\frac{dz}{d(x,z)d(z,u)}\right|
\leq C\{1+|\log d(x,u)|\}.
\]
The right side is square integrable in dimension two.  Hence the generated-target score has uniformly bounded \(L^2(P_g)\)-norm.  By (1) the harmonic variance and its Green cross-covariance are actually zero, which is stronger than the two asserted orders.  This completes the Frechet calculation and all ancillary conclusions.

Substitute \(h_n=n^{-a_h}\) and \(L_n=a_h\log n\).  The first requirement equals
\[
\frac{n^{1/2-a_h(s-2)}}{\sqrt{a_h\log n}}\longrightarrow0,
\]
which holds exactly when \(a_h\geq1/[2(s-2)]\); equality is allowed because the remaining factor is \((a_h\log n)^{-1/2}\).

The stochastic part of the second requirement is
\[
(\log n)^{1/2}n^{-1/2+(13/4)a_h},
\]
so it tends to zero exactly when \(a_h<2/13\).  Its deterministic part \(n^{-a_h(s-9/4)}\) tends to zero for \(a_h>0\) and \(s\geq8\).

Put
\[
A_n=\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{nh_n^{9/2}}},
\qquad B_n=h_n^{s-5/4}.
\]
The stochastic square in the third requirement is
\[
\sqrt{\frac n{L_n}}A_n^2
=a_h^{-1/2}(\log n)^{1/2}n^{-1/2+(9/2)a_h},
\]
and hence vanishes exactly for \(a_h<1/9\).  The deterministic square vanishes when
\(a_h\geq1/(4s-5)\), with equality again allowed by the logarithmic denominator.  The mixed term is, up to a fixed constant,
\[
\sqrt{\frac n{L_n}}A_nB_n
=a_h^{-1/2}n^{-a_h(s-7/2)},
\]
which vanishes for \(a_h>0\) and \(s\geq8\).  Finally,
\[
\frac1{2(s-2)}>\frac1{4s-5},
\qquad
\frac19<\frac2{13},
\]
and \(1/[2(s-2)]<1/9\) for \(s\geq8\).  Intersecting all necessary and sufficient inequalities therefore gives exactly
\[
\frac1{2(s-2)}\leq a_h<\frac19.
\]

Let \(t=f_{T1}\).  The parametrix calculation (8)--(9) in thm:uniform-critical-control shows that a unit-amplitude density noise with local intensity \(\mu(y_j)\) contributes
\[
\mu(y_j)\frac{B(y_j)^{-1}}{4\pi\sqrt{\det B(y_j)}}
\]
to the normalized diagonal covariance block.  We now compute the amplitude and intensity separately for all four samples, which is essential because the two control appearances are correlated within their own cells.

For a \(C0\) kernel tangent, the transformed noise is
\(\det(D(y))K_h^{\mathrm{per}}(R_0(y)-X)\), and the leading outer forcing multiplies it by \(-\alpha(y)\).  Changing variables \(x=R_0(y)\), its local design intensity in \(y\)-coordinates is
\[
f_{C0}(R_0(y))\det D(y)=\frac{t(y)}{\alpha(y)}.
\tag{16}
\]
For \(C1\), changing variables \(x=T(y)\) gives the same intensity because
\[
f_{C1}(T(y))\det H(y)=f_{C0}(R_0(y))\det D(y)=\frac{t(y)}{\alpha(y)}.
\tag{17}
\]
Both control amplitudes have absolute value \(\alpha(y)\), so each control cell has squared-amplitude times intensity \(\alpha(y)t(y)\).  For \(T0\), the corresponding intensity is
\[
f_{T0}(R_0(y))\det D(y)=t(y),
\tag{18}
\]
and for \(T1\) it is \(t(y)\); both amplitudes have absolute value one.  Mutual independence in ass:four-sample-design removes cross-cell covariances, but no within-cell term has been discarded.

After multiplication by the sample-ratio limits, the total local intensity is
\[
t(y_j)w_j,
\qquad
w_j=\alpha(y_j)(\rho_{C0}^{-1}+\rho_{C1}^{-1})
+\rho_{T0}^{-1}+\rho_{T1}^{-1}.
\tag{19}
\]
Since \(B=tH^{-1}\),
\[
t w_j\frac{B^{-1}}{4\pi\sqrt{\det B}}
=w_j\frac{\sqrt{\det H}\,H}{4\pi t}=V_j.
\tag{20}
\]
Distinct-grid covariances are \(o(1)\) after division by \(L_n\), by the separated-pole part of the parametrix proof.  The second elliptic score has bounded \(L^2\) norm, so its normalized variance is \(O(L_n^{-1})\); Cauchy--Schwarz bounds its normalized cross-covariance with the leading score by \(O(L_n^{-1/2})\).  The harmonic score is zero by thm:nested-derivative.  All bounds are uniform over \(\mathcal F_s\).  Equations (16)--(20) prove
\(\sup_P\lVert\Sigma_{h_n}(P)-V(P)\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\to0\).

On the event on which clipping is inactive, thm:uniform-critical-control and the sign change from the lifted map to the displacement give
\[
\widehat\tau-\tau(P)
=-\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}\frac1{n_g}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}
 \Psi_{g,h_n}(X_{g,i})+\operatorname{Bias}_{h_n}+\operatorname{Rem}_n.
\tag{21}
\]
where every score is centered under \(P_g\),
\(\sqrt{n/L_n}\operatorname{Bias}_{h_n}=o(1)\), and
\(\sqrt{n/L_n}\operatorname{Rem}_n=o_{\mathbb P}(1)\), uniformly over \(\mathcal F_s\).  The stray sign in (21) has no effect on covariance.

The smoothed inverse-distance kernel bounds imply, uniformly in \(g\) and \(P\),
\[
\mathbb E_P\lVert\Psi_{g,h_n}(X)\rVert^2\leq C L_n,
\quad
\mathbb E_P\lVert\Psi_{g,h_n}(X)\rVert^3\leq C h_n^{-1},
\quad
\mathbb E_P\lVert\Psi_{g,h_n}(X)\rVert^4\leq C h_n^{-2}.
\tag{22}
\]
The third absolute-moment sum for the normalized array in (21) is at most
\[
C\left(\frac n{L_n}\right)^{3/2}
 \sum_g\frac{n_g}{n_g^3h_n}
\leq \frac{C}{\sqrt n\,h_nL_n^{3/2}}\longrightarrow0,
\tag{23}
\]
because \(n_g\geq n\) and \(a_h<1/9\).  Taylor expansion of each centered summand's characteristic function has a third-order remainder bounded by its third absolute moment.  Equation (23) makes the sum of those remainders vanish uniformly, while the quadratic terms converge by ass:cell-ratios and lem:full-critical-covariance to the characteristic function of \(N(0,V(P))\).  For any function bounded by one and with Lipschitz constant one, adding the two remainders in (21) changes its expectation by at most their norm.  This proves the displayed uniform bounded-Lipschitz convergence directly.

Uniform elliptic stability and (10)--(11) also give \(C^1\) consistency of \(\widehat p\) and \(\widehat T\).  Since every population graph and translation coordinate is separated from its branch boundary by more than \(\beta\), the regular branch is selected whenever this error is below \(\beta/2\).  The complement has probability \(o(1)\) uniformly.  Hence the total measurable fallback is asymptotically irrelevant, as claimed.

We compare the proposed estimator first with the empirical covariance of the oracle finite-bandwidth scores and then with its expectation.  Conditional on an opposite-fold pilot, thm:uniform-critical-control gives
\[
\max_{g,r}\frac{\lVert\widehat\Psi_{g,h_n}^{(-r)}-\Psi_{g,h_n}\rVert_{L^2(P_g)}}{\sqrt{L_n}}
=o_{\mathbb P}(1).
\tag{24}
\]
For the oracle scores, (22) implies
\[
\mathbb E\left\lVert
 \frac1{n_gL_n}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}
 \left\{\Psi_{g,h_n}(X_{g,i})\Psi_{g,h_n}(X_{g,i})^{\mathsf T}
 -\mathbb E[\Psi_{g,h_n}(X)\Psi_{g,h_n}(X)^{\mathsf T}]\right\}
 \right\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2
\leq \frac{C}{n_gh_n^2L_n^2}=o(1),
\tag{25}
\]
entry by entry; fixed \(J\) converts this to operator norm.  Subtracting the within-fold mean changes the left side by the outer product of an empirical mean, whose normalized size is \(O_{\mathbb P}(n_g^{-1})\).

Cross-fitting makes the score error in (24) independent of its evaluation fold.  Conditional Cauchy--Schwarz therefore bounds the normalized difference of the estimated and oracle covariance matrices by
\[
\frac{\lVert\widehat\Psi-\Psi\rVert_2}{\sqrt{L_n}}
\left\{
2\frac{\lVert\Psi\rVert_2}{\sqrt{L_n}}
+\frac{\lVert\widehat\Psi-\Psi\rVert_2}{\sqrt{L_n}}
\right\}=o_{\mathbb P}(1),
\tag{26}
\]
uniformly over cells and folds.  Equations (25)--(26), \(n/n_g\to\rho_g^{-1}\), and lem:full-critical-covariance prove
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal F_s}\mathbb P_P
 \left(\lVert\widehat V_{\mathrm{adj}}-V(P)\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}>\varepsilon\right)
\longrightarrow0.
\]
All finite-bandwidth cross products, including those between the two control appearances, were retained in (24)--(26).  The harmonic component is zero on the regular branch; even under the displayed bounded-score formulation its variance divided by \(L_n\) and its cross-covariance divided by \(L_n\) vanish by Cauchy--Schwarz.

Because \(\theta_n=n^{-1}\),
\[
\lVert\widehat V_{\mathrm{adj}}^R-V(P)\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
\leq\lVert\widehat V_{\mathrm{adj}}-V(P)\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}+n^{-1},
\]
which proves the second consistency assertion.  Finally, positivity and ellipticity give the uniform lower eigenvalue bound
\[
\lambda_{\min}(V_j(P))
\geq \frac{\lambda^2}{4\pi C\bar\rho}>0.
\tag{27}
\]
On the event where the covariance error is smaller than half this constant, multiplying out \(A^{-1}-B^{-1}=A^{-1}(B-A)B^{-1}\) yields
\[
\lVert(\widehat V_{\mathrm{adj},jj}^R)^{-1}-V_j(P)^{-1}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
\leq C\lVert\widehat V_{\mathrm{adj},jj}^R-V_j(P)\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}.
\]
Taking the maximum over fixed \(J\) proves the inverse assertion.  Adding the positive ridge makes the full matrix, and hence every principal block, positive definite in every sample.

Positive semidefiniteness of the empirical outer-product matrix and \(\theta_n>0\) imply
\(\widehat V_{\mathrm{adj}}^R\succ0\) in every sample.  Thus every principal block is invertible and the maximum defining \(\widehat c_{1-\gamma}\) is a finite nonnegative random variable, so its conditional quantile exists.

Conditionally on the data, Gaussianity and independence of the multipliers give exactly
\[
Z^\star\mid\{X_{g,i}\}\sim N(0,\widehat V_{\mathrm{adj}}).
\tag{28}
\]
Indeed its covariance is
\[
\frac n{L_n}\sum_g\frac1{n_g^2}\sum_i
(\widehat\Psi_{g,i}-\overline\Psi_{g,r(i)})
(\widehat\Psi_{g,i}-\overline\Psi_{g,r(i)})^{\mathsf T}
=\widehat V_{\mathrm{adj}}.
\]
This is exactly the displayed definition of \(\widehat V_{\mathrm{adj}}\).

By thm:adjoint-covariance, both \(\widehat V_{\mathrm{adj}}\) and its ridged version converge uniformly to \(V(P)\).  Hence (28), continuity of Gaussian laws in their covariance matrices, and the inverse conclusion of that theorem imply conditional convergence of the multiplier maximum to
\[
M_P=\max_{1\leq j\leq J}Z_j^{\mathsf T}V_j(P)^{-1}Z_j,
\qquad Z\sim N(0,V(P)).
\tag{29}
\]
The matrix \(V(P)\) is block diagonal and positive definite, so the terms in (29) are independent \(\chi^2_2\) variables.  Therefore \(M_P\) has the continuous distribution function
\((1-e^{-x/2})^J\) for \(x\geq0\), independent of \(P\).  Conditional quantiles consequently converge uniformly to its unique \((1-\gamma)\)-quantile.

The joint critical CLT and covariance consistency give the same limit (29) for
\[
\max_j\frac n{L_n}(\widehat\tau_j-\tau_j(P))^{\mathsf T}
(\widehat V_{\mathrm{adj},jj}^R)^{-1}(\widehat\tau_j-\tau_j(P)).
\]
Comparing this statistic with the consistent conditional quantile proves simultaneous coverage tending to \(1-\gamma\), uniformly over \(\mathcal F_s\).

We prove the proposed, honestly center-local version.  Let \(x_\star\) be the preimage in cell \(g_\star\) of the pole \(y_1\).  Equations (8)--(9), after scalarization by the nonzero vector \(\upsilon\), give
\[
\varphi_{g_\star}(x)
=\frac{b^{\mathsf T}(x-x_\star)}{(x-x_\star)^{\mathsf T}Q(x-x_\star)}
+O(1+|\log d(x,x_\star)|),
\tag{30}
\]
where \(Q\succ0\) and \(b\neq0\).  The nonzero conclusion follows because every pullback Jacobian and \(B(y_1)^{-1}\) is invertible and every leading cell weight is nonzero.  Polar integration in (30), density positivity, and the annular definition of \(\chi_\varepsilon\) yield
\[
c_1\log(1/\varepsilon)\leq\lVert\ell_{\varepsilon,g_\star}\rVert_2^2
\leq c_2\log(1/\varepsilon).
\tag{31}
\]
Differentiating the cutoff and the inverse-distance term at most \(s\) times gives
\[
\lVert f_{0g_\star}\ell_{\varepsilon,g_\star}\rVert_{C^s}
\leq C_{P_0}\varepsilon^{-s-1}.
\tag{32}
\]

Put \(L_\varepsilon=\lVert\ell_{\varepsilon,g_\star}\rVert_2\) and
\(u_n=\zeta\ell_{\varepsilon_n,g_\star}/(\sqrt n L_{\varepsilon_n})\).  Centering gives \(\int f_{0g_\star}u_n=0\), hence both alternatives integrate to one.  Equations (31)--(32) show
\[
\lVert f_{0g_\star}u_n\rVert_{C^s}
\leq \frac{C_{P_0}\zeta n^{-1/2+\eta(s+1)}}{\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon_n)}}=o(1).
\tag{33}
\]
The same bound in supremum norm shows \(\lVert u_n\rVert_\infty=o(1)\), so the two densities are positive.  Because \(P_0\) is an interior point, (33) preserves all density and ellipticity inequalities and the positive branch and cut margins for sufficiently large \(n\); this is precisely where dependence on the center's interior margin is necessary.

For \(|u_n|\leq1/2\), the elementary inequalities
\((\sqrt{1+u}-1)^2\leq u^2\) and
\((\sqrt{1+u}-\sqrt{1-u})^2\leq4u^2\) give
\[
\operatorname{Hel}^2(P_{n,\pm,g_\star},P_{0g_\star})\leq\frac{\zeta^2}{n},
\qquad
\operatorname{Hel}^2(P_{n,+,g_\star},P_{n,-,g_\star})\leq\frac{4\zeta^2}{n}.
\tag{34}
\]
For product laws the Hellinger affinity factors exactly:
\[
\int\sqrt{d\bigotimes_iP_i\,d\bigotimes_iQ_i}
=\prod_i\int\sqrt{dP_i\,dQ_i}.
\]
Thus the product squared Hellinger distance is at most the sum of the component squared distances.  Together with \(n_{g_\star}=n\) and a smaller fixed \(\zeta_0\), (34) implies both neighborhood membership and the stated product-experiment bound.

For structural membership, set
\[
h_0=\operatorname{id},\quad \nu_C=P_{n,\pm,C0},\quad
\nu_T=P_{n,\pm,T0},\quad h_1=p,\quad h_{1\star}=T^{-1}\circ p.
\]
Then \(h_1\#\nu_C=P_{n,\pm,C1}\) and
\[
h_{1\star}\#\nu_T=T^{-1}\#(p\#P_{n,\pm,T0})=P_{n,\pm,T1}.
\]
Moreover \(h_1\circ h_0^{-1}=p\) and
\(h_1\circ h_{1\star}^{-1}=T\); both graphs are cyclically monotone by their definition as optimal maps.  Equation (33) and the interior margins preserve diffeomorphism and regularity.  The harmonic translations are zero by the cut-free argument in thm:nested-derivative.

Choose the Riesz representative centered under \(P_{0g_\star}\).  Then (30)--(31) imply
\[
\int\varphi_{g_\star}\ell_{\varepsilon,g_\star}\,dP_{0g_\star}
=\int\chi_\varepsilon\varphi_{g_\star}^2,dP_{0g_\star}
\geq c\log(1/\varepsilon).
\tag{35}
\]
Applying the tame bound (15) to the two opposite paths gives a remainder bounded by
\[
C\frac{\zeta^2}{n\log(1/\varepsilon_n)}\varepsilon_n^{-9/2}
=o\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon_n)}n}\right),
\tag{36}
\]
because \(\eta<1/[2(s+1)]\leq1/18<1/9\).  The linear terms, (31), and (35) yield
\[
\left|\upsilon^{\mathsf T}\{\tau(P_{n,+})-\tau(P_{n,-})\}_1\right|
\geq \frac{2c\zeta\log(1/\varepsilon_n)}{\sqrt n L_{\varepsilon_n}}
+o\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon_n)}n}\right),
\]
which proves the desired separation after reducing the positive constant.

For the upper bound, square expansion (21).  The covariance calculation and (22) give
\[
\mathbb E_P\left\lVert\sum_g\frac1{n_g}\sum_i\Psi_{g,h_n}(X_{g,i})\right\rVert^2
\leq C\frac{L_n}{n}.
\tag{37}
\]
The exponential-moment mesh proof of (10)--(11) also gives the corresponding second-moment bounds.  Thus (15) and lem:bandwidth-feasibility imply that the squared bias and expected squared remainder are \(o(L_n/n)\).  The clipping complement has probability at most \(C\exp(-c_0nh_n^2)\), while the translation-aware torus displacement and its fallback are bounded; its risk contribution is therefore \(o(L_n/n)\).  Combining these bounds proves the asserted uniform upper risk.

For the converse, use the two laws of the proposed version of lem:green-local-alternatives with \(\zeta\) small enough that their product-experiment total variation distance is at most \(1/2\).  Indeed, writing the two product densities as \(p\) and \(q\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives \(\int|p-q|\leq\{\int(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\}^{1/2}\{\int(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)^2\}^{1/2}\), so (34) gives this conclusion after reducing \(\zeta\).  Let
\[
\Delta_n=\left|\upsilon^{\mathsf T}\{\tau(P_{n,+})-\tau(P_{n,-})\}_1\right|.
\]
For any vector estimator, projection on this scalar coordinate and the two disjoint events where its error is smaller than \(\Delta_n/2\) give the elementary two-point testing inequality
\[
\max_{\sigma\in\{+,-\}}
\mathbb E_{P_{n,\sigma}}\lVert\widetilde\tau_n-\tau(P_{n,\sigma})\rVert^2
\geq \frac{\Delta_n^2}{16}\{1-\operatorname{TV}(P_{n,+}^{(n)},P_{n,-}^{(n)})\}
\geq \frac{\Delta_n^2}{32}.
\tag{38}
\]
Both laws belong to \(\mathcal N_n(P_0,\kappa)\), and the separation lemma gives
\[
\Delta_n^2\geq c\zeta^2\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon_n)}n
=c\zeta^2\frac{\eta}{a_h}\frac{L_n}{n}.
\tag{39}
\]
Taking the supremum, then the infimum over all estimators, and finally the lower limit in (38)--(39) proves the lower bound with a strictly positive \(c_0\).

If every cell law is uniform, the identity map is a zero-cost feasible transport and is therefore the unique optimal map almost everywhere.  Hence \(p=T=R_0=\operatorname{id}\), \(S=H=D=I_2\), \(\alpha=1\), and \(A=B=\mathsf C=I_2\).  The second term in def:nested-derivative vanishes because \(\nabla\alpha=0\), and the harmonic term vanishes by thm:nested-derivative.  Thus
\[
\mathcal D_P[\delta]=\nabla(-\Delta)^{-1}
(-\delta_{C0}+\delta_{C1}+\delta_{T0}-\delta_{T1}).
\]
For one cell, Fourier inversion gives
\[
\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{0\}}
\frac{mm^{\mathsf T}}{4\pi^2|m|^4}|\widehat K(hm)|^2
=\frac{I_2}{4\pi}\log(1/h)+O(1),
\]
where the angular integral is \(\int_{\mathbb S^1}\omega\omega^{\mathsf T}d\omega=\pi I_2\).  Four independent, equally sized cells add their variances, giving \(V_j=4I_2/(4\pi)=I_2/\pi\).  If only the \(T1\) law is sampled and the source is fixed, only one summand remains, giving \(I_2/(4\pi)\).

The Jacobians of the three production maps at \(u\) are
\[
Dh_0^{\mathrm{sep}}=I_2,
\quad Dh_1^{\mathrm{sep}}=\operatorname{diag}(1+0.2\cos(2\pi u_1),1),
\]
\[
Dh_{1\star}^{\mathrm{sep}}
=\operatorname{diag}(1+0.3\cos(2\pi u_1),1-0.1\cos(2\pi u_2)).
\]
Their eigenvalues lie respectively in \([1,1]\), \([0.8,1.2]\), and \([0.7,1.3]\); hence all three maps are periodic diffeomorphisms.  Their displayed lifts are gradients of strictly convex Euclidean lifts.  The corresponding periodic potentials have zero mean and equal
\[
\phi_{h_1}(u)=-\frac{0.1}{2\pi^2}\cos(2\pi u_1),
\qquad
\phi_{h_{1\star}}(u)=-\frac{0.15}{2\pi^2}\cos(2\pi u_1)
+\frac{0.05}{2\pi^2}\cos(2\pi u_2).
\]
Thus their selected translations are zero.

Since \(h_0\) is the identity and both latent laws are uniform,
\(f_{C0}=f_{T0}=1\), \(p=h_1^{\mathrm{sep}}\), and
\(T=h_1^{\mathrm{sep}}\circ(h_{1\star}^{\mathrm{sep}})^{-1}\).  At \(y=h_{1\star}^{\mathrm{sep}}(u)\),
\[
H(y)=\operatorname{diag}\left(
\frac{1+0.2\cos(2\pi u_1)}{1+0.3\cos(2\pi u_1)},
\frac1{1-0.1\cos(2\pi u_2)}\right)\succ0.
\]
The first eigenvalue lies in \([12/13,8/7]\) and the second in \([10/11,10/9]\).  The pushforward densities lie between the reciprocals of the displayed positive Jacobian determinants; in particular
\(100/143\leq f_{T1}\leq100/63\).  All functions are smooth.  Choosing the class constants to contain these ranges and choosing \(\beta\) below the positive displacement and cut margins proves membership in \(\mathcal F_s\).  The maps \(p\) and \(T\) have positive symmetric Jacobians, so their equivariant Euclidean lifts are gradients of convex functions.  Fenchel's inequality applied to every lattice translate gives torus dual potentials attaining equality on their graphs; hence those graphs are \(c_{\mathbb T}\)-cyclically monotone and ass:cic-identification is met.

At \(u=(1/4,1/4)\), all cosines vanish and
\[
y-T(y)=h_{1\star}^{\mathrm{sep}}(u)-h_1^{\mathrm{sep}}(u)
=\left(\frac{0.05}{\pi},-\frac{0.05}{\pi}\right)\neq0.
\]
At the same point \(H(y)=I_2\), \(f_{T1}(y)=1\), and \(\alpha(y)=1\).  Equal cell sizes give \(w_j=4\), and lem:full-critical-covariance yields \(V_j=I_2/\pi\), as claimed.

theorem.statement:
Uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal F_s\), the pole-parametrix construction in \(\mathfrak H_{\mathrm{crit}}\) gives the frozen-pole logarithmic covariance for the variable-coefficient, transformed-kernel Green response.  The second elliptic term of \(\mathcal D_P\) and the harmonic term \(\mathcal H_P\) have uniformly bounded cellwise \(L^2(P_g)\) scores.  For the opposite-fold pilots used in \(\widehat\Psi_{g,h_n}^{(-r)}\),
\[
\max_{g\in\mathcal G,\ r\in\{1,2\}}\frac{\lVert\widehat\Psi_{g,h_n}^{(-r)}-\Psi_{g,h_n}\rVert_{L^2(P_g)}}{\sqrt{L_n}}
=o_{\mathbb P}(1),
\]
uniformly in the fold.  Finally the nested plug-in expansion has deterministic bias \(O(h_n^{s-2})\) and a remainder that is \(o_{\mathbb P}(\sqrt{L_n/n})\), uniformly over \(\mathcal F_s\).
theorem.proof_tex:
We prove the four assertions in the order in which they enter the stochastic expansion.

First consider \(\mathcal L_B=-\operatorname{div}(B\nabla)\), and let \(G_B(y,z)\) be its mean-zero Green function.  At a pole \(y\), put \(B_y=B(y)\) and
\[
\Gamma_y(z)=-\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{\det B_y}}
 \log\left|B_y^{-1/2}(z-y)\right|.
\]
Choose a cutoff supported inside the common injectivity radius.  Applying \(\mathcal L_B\) to the cutoff fundamental solution shows that
\(R_y(z)=G_B(y,z)-\Gamma_y(z)\) solves an equation whose only singular part is
\[
\operatorname{div}\{(B(z)-B_y)\nabla\Gamma_y(z)\}.
\]
Uniform \(C^1\) bounds and ellipticity give \(|B(z)-B_y|\leq C|z-y|\),
\(|\nabla\Gamma_y(z)|\leq C|z-y|^{-1}\), and
\(|D^2\Gamma_y(z)|\leq C|z-y|^{-2}\).  Representing the residual solution once more by a Green kernel and splitting the integral into the three regions used in the proof of thm:nested-derivative gives
\[
|\nabla_zR_y(z)|\leq C\{1+|\log d_{\mathbb T^2}(y,z)|\}.
\tag{8}
\]
Every constant is uniform over \(\mathcal F_s\): differentiating the two Monge--Ampere identities and using their uniformly elliptic coefficient matrices recursively bounds the needed coefficient derivatives by the fixed density, positivity, and ellipticity constants.

The singular part therefore controls the logarithm.  With \(z-y=B_y^{1/2}r\omega\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{ch<|B_y^{-1/2}(z-y)|<c_0}
 \nabla\Gamma_y(z)\nabla\Gamma_y(z)^{\mathsf T}\,dz
&=\frac{B_y^{-1/2}}{4\pi^2\sqrt{\det B_y}}
 \left(\int_{\mathbb S^1}\omega\omega^{\mathsf T}\,d\omega\right)
 B_y^{-1/2}\int_{ch}^{c_0}\frac{dr}{r}\\
&=\frac{B_y^{-1}}{4\pi\sqrt{\det B_y}}\log(1/h)+O(1).
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]
The region within \(O(h)\) of the pole contributes \(O(1)\), because the smoothed gradient is \(O(h^{-1})\) on an area \(O(h^2)\).  On the intermediate region, the unit mass and vanishing moments of the kernel make the difference from the unsmoothed gradient integrable with squared integral \(o(\log(1/h))\); outside a fixed ball all kernels are uniformly bounded.  Estimate (8), whose square is locally integrable, changes (9) only by \(o(\log(1/h))\).  Smooth diffeomorphic pullbacks merely replace the inner kernel ball by a uniformly nondegenerate ellipse and its density by its value at the pole, so the coefficient in (9) is unchanged.  Two distinct grid poles remain uniformly separated under \(T\) and \(R_0\), by ellipticity and ass:fixed-separated-grid; the product of their two inverse-distance singularities is integrable.  Their covariance is therefore \(O(1)=o(L_n)\).

The second elliptic term has the kernel
\[
u\longmapsto\int \nabla_yG_B(y,z)^{\mathsf T}
 (\mathsf C\nabla\alpha)(z)\nabla_zG_{\mathsf C}(z,u)\,dz.
\]
The three-region convolution estimate proves that it is bounded by
\(C\{1+|\log d(y,u)|\}\); hence its \(L^2(P_g)\)-norm is uniformly bounded.  The proof of thm:nested-derivative gives \(\mathcal H_P=0\) on the regular intrinsic-cost branch, so its score is also uniformly bounded.

Next consider estimated scores.  Differentiation of a periodized empirical kernel sum, followed by the exponential Markov bound for its bounded centered summands on a mesh of spacing \(h_n^{s+3}\) and the deterministic derivative bound between mesh points, gives, for \(\beta=1/4\),
\[
\max_g\lVert\widehat f_g-f_g\rVert_{C^{1,\beta}}
=O_{\mathbb P}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{nh_n^{9/2}}}+h_n^{s-5/4}\right),
\tag{10}
\]
and
\[
\max_g\lVert\widehat f_g-f_g\rVert_{C^{2,\beta}}
=O_{\mathbb P}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{nh_n^{13/2}}}+h_n^{s-9/4}\right)=o_{\mathbb P}(1).
\tag{11}
\]
The clipping event is contained in the complement of
\(\max_g\lVert\widetilde f_g-f_g\rVert_\infty<c/2\), whose probability is at most
\(C\exp(-c_0nh_n^2)\); on the latter event clipping and renormalization are exactly inactive.  Uniform elliptic stability applied to the differentiated Monge--Ampere equations transfers (10)--(11) to the maps, coefficients, and their first derivatives.  In particular every estimated pole differs from its population pole by
\[
O_{\mathbb P}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{nh_n^{9/2}}}+h_n^{s-5/4}\right)=o_{\mathbb P}(h_n),
\tag{12}
\]
where the last relation follows from \(a_h<1/9\).

Subtracting two cutoff parametrices proves the deterministic stability estimate
\[
\frac{\lVert\widehat\Psi_{g,h}-\Psi_{g,h}\rVert_2}{\sqrt{\log(1/h)}}
\leq C\left(\lVert\widehat B-B\rVert_{C^1}
+\lVert\widehat{\mathsf C}-\mathsf C\rVert_{C^1}
+\lVert\widehat\alpha-\alpha\rVert_{C^1}
+\frac{|\widehat y-y|}{h}\right)+o(1).
\tag{13}
\]
Indeed coefficient differences multiply the inverse-distance singularity and hence have norm \(O(\sqrt{\log(1/h)})\), whereas differentiating the smoothed pole gives norm \(O(h^{-1})\).  Equations (11)--(12) in (13) give the asserted opposite-fold score convergence.  Cross-fitting makes the pilots independent of the observations on which this norm is evaluated.

Finally subtract the two inner and outer Monge--Ampere equations.  In dimension two the exact identity
\[
\det(M+E)-\det M=\operatorname{cof}(M):E+\det E
\tag{14}
\]
shows that every non-linear determinant term is quadratic in the second derivatives of the map increment.  Expanding the exact generated-density identity
\[
\widehat f_q(z)=\widehat f_{C1}(z)
 \left(\widehat f_{T0}/\widehat f_{C0}\right)(\widehat p^{-1}(z))
\]
shows similarly that each term not present in \(\mathcal D_P\) contains two increments.  More explicitly, if \(U\) is the inner-map increment minus its linear solution and \(W\) is the analogous outer remainder, subtraction of the two exact equations and (14) give
\[
\mathcal L_AU=R_A,
\qquad
\mathcal L_BW=R_B+\operatorname{div}(E\nabla U),
\]
where, on the event in (11), coefficient positivity and the product rule give
\[
\lVert R_A\rVert_{C^{0,1/4}}+
\lVert R_B\rVert_{C^{0,1/4}}+
\lVert E\rVert_{C^{1,1/4}}\lVert U\rVert_{C^{2,1/4}}
\leq C\left(\max_g\lVert\widehat f_g-f_g\rVert_{C^{1,1/4}}\right)^2.
\]
The normalized inverse estimates for these two uniformly elliptic equations consequently give the tame bound
\[
\left\lVert\widehat T-T-\mathcal D_P[\widehat f-f]\right\rVert_{\mathcal Y_J}
\leq C\left(\max_g\lVert\widehat f_g-f_g\rVert_{C^{1,1/4}}\right)^2,
\tag{15}
\]
provided the \(C^{2,1/4}\) norm in (11) is below a fixed constant.  This event has probability tending to one uniformly.  The deterministic kernel bias propagated through the same linear equations is \(O(h_n^{s-2})\).  Substitution of (10) into (15) gives exactly the third scale expression in lem:bandwidth-feasibility, while the bias gives its first expression.  That lemma therefore yields
\[
\sqrt{n/L_n}\,\lVert\operatorname{Bias}_{h_n}\rVert=o(1),
\qquad
\sqrt{n/L_n}\,\lVert\operatorname{Rem}_n\rVert=o_{\mathbb P}(1).
\]
This proves every assertion in the resolved question.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed:
For each fixed \(P_0\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal F_s)\), there are constants \(c_1,c_2,C_{P_0},\zeta_0>0\) and a sample threshold, allowed to depend on the interior margin of \(P_0\), such that
\[
c_1\log(1/\varepsilon)\leq
\lVert\ell_{\varepsilon,g_\star}\rVert_{L^2(P_{0g_\star})}^2
\leq c_2\log(1/\varepsilon),
\qquad
\lVert f_{0g_\star}\ell_{\varepsilon,g_\star}\rVert_{C^s}
\leq C_{P_0}\varepsilon^{-s-1}.
\]
For every fixed \(0<\zeta\leq\zeta_0\) satisfying \(C_{P_0}\zeta^2\leq\kappa\), the laws from def:green-local-alternatives obey \(P_{n,+},P_{n,-}\in\mathcal F_s\cap\mathcal N_n(P_0,\kappa)\),
\[
\operatorname{Hel}^2\left(\bigotimes_{g\in\mathcal G}P_{n,+,g}^{\otimes n_g},
\bigotimes_{g\in\mathcal G}P_{n,-,g}^{\otimes n_g}\right)
\leq C_{P_0}\zeta^2\leq1/2,
\]
and
\[
\left|\upsilon^{\mathsf T}\{\tau(P_{n,+})-\tau(P_{n,-})\}_1\right|
\geq c_1\zeta\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon_n)}n}.
\]
The restriction \(\eta<1/[2(s+1)]\) makes the \(C^s\) perturbation vanish, and perturbing the cell with \(n_{g_\star}=n\) makes the product-Hellinger bound independent of the other cell-size ratios.  For each sign, causal-class membership is witnessed by \(h_0=\operatorname{id}\), \(\nu_C=P_{n,\pm,C0}\), \(\nu_T=P_{n,\pm,T0}\), \(h_1=p\), and \(h_{1\star}=T^{-1}\circ p\).  For all sufficiently large \(n\), with the threshold allowed to depend on the interior margin of \(P_0\), these maps retain the required diffeomorphism and ellipticity properties, and their graphs remain separated from \(\operatorname{Cut}_{\mathbb T}\).  Moreover,
\[
\lVert a_p(P_{n,\pm})-a_p(P_0)\rVert+
\lVert a_T(P_{n,\pm})-a_T(P_0)\rVert=O(n^{-1/2}),
\]
so the harmonic translation changes are negligible relative to the displayed Green separation.

The two graphs required by the structural representation are \(c_{\mathbb T}\)-cyclically monotone.
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The frozen claim asks for constants uniform over every interior center, but the interior-point assumption supplies only a center-specific positive margin and no uniform lower bound on those margins. The proof closes for each fixed center, which is exactly what the local minimax theorem uses.
